intended_object: For a Dedekind domain R and a set S of nonzero primes (height-one primes), the property that an integral ideal I is nonzero and coprime to S, meaning no 𝔭 ∈ S divides I. These are the integral ideals in the group I^S of ideals prime to S used in class field theory and for Dirichlet/Hecke L-series. Inferred from the docstring, the module documentation and how the library uses it (integralIdealsAway, characters' bad primes).
explanation: The body is exactly `I ≠ ⊥ ∧ ∀ 𝔭 ∈ S, ¬ 𝔭.asIdeal ∣ I`, which is what the docstring says. In a Dedekind domain every 𝔭 in the height-one spectrum is maximal, so for a nonzero I, "𝔭 does not divide I" is the same as "𝔭 does not contain I", and the same as 𝔭 + I = R. So this is the usual "prime to S" condition. Requiring I to be nonzero matches the standard setting: the group I^S consists of nonzero (fractional) ideals coprime to S. The docstring states this convention explicitly, and the library relies on it, for example in the induction principle and in the submonoid `integralIdealsAway`. The degenerate cases come out right: with S = ∅ the condition is just I ≠ ⊥, with S = univ it forces I = ⊤, and ⊤ is prime to every S. Only `CommRing R` is assumed, which is at least as general as the Dedekind setting, so the definition is not too narrow. Mathlib has no dedicated predicate for this notion.
